ideas.name: braced long slide
ideas.description: The long_slide jaw (sector radius 50 mm: up to 103 mm opening, face parallel, tip +1 mm, 32 N at every width), changed to remove its two failure modes. (1) A printed outer bridge clamps the far ends of both 3 x 150 mm rods, so they are supported at both ends instead of sticking out 94 mm. That removes the tilting load that puts 138 N on each bushing. (2) A pair of MR63 bearings act as backing rollers behind the rack, right at the gear sector, so the rack cannot lift more than 0.1 mm off the gear. The catalogue version lifts 2.2 mm at 85 mm, and the teeth skip past 0.5 mm. (3) Four LM3UU bushings in two pairs spaced 30 mm apart share the load.
ideas.test: Add a jaw type to the simulator: the long_slide carriage with rods clamped at both ends, contacts for backing rollers behind the rack, and four bushings. Check rack lift and bushing load at 85-96 mm and the squeeze on the mustard bottle (96 mm, 431 g, friction 0.4: needs 2*0.4*N > 4.2 N with margin, and the design gives 32 N). Also check the arm's shoulder torque: 0.41 + 0.15*4.31 + the slide's extra mass, against 1.62 N*m.

ideas.name: rocker pad (convex-crowned jaw pad)
ideas.description: A printed pad whose face, seen from the side, is a circular arc of about 40 mm radius spanning normals from about -25 deg to +65 deg on the moving jaw, with a TPU skin. A flat wedge is parallel to the fixed face at only one opening. On a convex face, the point whose normal is horizontal always exists, so the contact on a vertical box side is antipodal (no N sin a squeeze-out) at every opening from 17 to 95 mm. The arc runs down to the pad's lowest point, so at wide openings (where the jaw has turned 45-60 deg) the horizontal-normal point sits near the bottom of the pad. That puts the contact below the tops of low wide objects (pudding +19, tuna +17, sugar +23), while at narrow openings the contact moves up the pad and the heel stays out of the way (fixes the banana conflict). A lower arc, kept within the jaw's footprint, gives mustard the fingertip drop it needs at 96 mm, provided the opening stays at or above the stock 95 mm.
ideas.test: Simulator needs a pads variant with a curved (arc) face profile on the moving jaw: parameters arc_radius_mm and normal span (deg). The contact solver must track the moving contact point along the arc, and the interference check must cover the arc at the closed limit (-0.16 rad).

ideas.name: self-aligning pivot pad (moving jaw)
ideas.description: A replacement for the moving-jaw pad. A printed PLA shoe bolts to the moving jaw with the existing 4 m2 screws at the current 30° wedge. A separate printed face plate with a 1.5 mm TPU skin pivots on an m3 screw used as a pin, running through a printed bushing. The pivot axis is horizontal along the 12 mm pad width and lies in the contact plane about 5 mm above the toe. A printed TPU flexure, two 1 mm webs between shoe and plate, centres the plate at the 30° pose, with hard stops at ±35°. The fixed pad stays as it is, since its face is already vertical. When a flat side presses an edge of the tilted plate, the off-pivot load rotates the plate flat against the wall, so the contact normal is horizontal at any opening. A contact at the pivot, as on spheres, makes no moment and keeps the 30° behaviour that holds the current 17 groups. Added wrist mass is about 4 g.
ideas.test: In the gripper model, split the moving pad into two bodies. The shoe stays fixed to the moving jaw at pad_angle_deg=30. The face plate (TPU friction 0.9, 1.5 mm skin) is joined to it by a hinge whose axis runs along the pad width and lies on the face surface 5 mm above the toe. Give the hinge a torsional spring of about 0.05 N·m/rad centred at 0, joint limits ±35°, and light damping. Run all 21 groups, re-tuning with System 1, and check the no-interference law for the plate against the fixed pad over the -0.17..1.20 rad range of the jaw.

ideas.name: levelled moving pad (pad-levelling link on the stock revolute jaw)
ideas.description: A printed pad carrier carries the TPU-faced moving pad and turns on a 3 mm pin with an MR63 bearing at the stock moving fingertip. A printed levelling link of about 75 mm goes from a second MR63 pin at the top of the carrier to an M3 pin on the gripper body, offset from the servo hinge by the same vector. The jaw, the link, the carrier and the body form a parallelogram, so the pad face keeps a vertical orientation at every servo angle from -0.17 to 1.20 rad. The fixed pad stays the current printed pad with its TPU skin. The design keeps the stock hinge radius of 81 mm, the 94 mm opening and the 20 N squeeze. What changes is the moving face angle at each opening: today it runs from -22 deg at 17 mm to +29 deg at 85 mm, and with the link it is 0 deg everywhere. The toe still rises by R(1 - cos q) (+23 mm at 85 mm), so the gains depend on System 1 putting the toe below the top of the box. At the depths it already found, the toe sits 3 to 8 mm below the top.
ideas.test: Add a pads variant 'levelled' to the simulator. The moving pad's orientation is fixed vertical in the world frame instead of turning with the jaw (pad_angle tracks the jaw angle). The pad pivot sits at the stock fingertip, and the link is a body checked for interference against the fixed pad shoe at jaw -0.17 rad and against the wrist over its roll range. Then rerun all 21 groups with System 1 retuning the grasp.

ideas.name: mid-arc parallelogram jaw (offset-hung finger, sag-balanced)
ideas.description: Two printed 100 mm links run from the gripper servo horn and from a second frame pivot, offset parallel to it, to a coupler. This is a four-bar parallelogram, so the moving finger never rotates and its face stays parallel to the fixed jaw at every opening. The difference from the catalogue parallelogram: the finger is an L-bracket hung from the coupler about 28 mm toward the open side, and the horn is indexed so the links are vertical when the jaws are 58.5 mm apart. The fingertip then runs along the lowest part of its 100 mm circle across the whole 17–100 mm working range, rising at most 9 mm between the middle and either end. The finger's toe is extended 4.5 mm below that lowest point, which splits the remaining error into ±4.5 mm against the fixed fingertip. The face is a flat vertical TPU-skinned pad (the existing pads at pad_angle 0, groove 0, 12 mm wide). Maximum opening is 100 mm (mustard is 96 mm). Squeeze is servo torque over L cos θ, about 16–18 N. Each pivot runs on an MR63 bearing pair on an M3 screw.
ideas.test: A parallelogram jaw variant in the simulator with two extra geometry parameters. The first is the finger's horizontal offset from the coupler (or, equivalently, the opening at which the links are vertical), range 30–70 mm. The second is the finger's drop below the arc's lowest point, range 0–8 mm. link_mm should extend to 120. Mechanism-law checks are needed for link sweep against the wrist at every wrist roll (the long_slide sector failed this) and for the finger against the fixed jaw at the closed end. Then run all 21 objects with the TPU pads at pad_angle 0.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=1.5, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=45, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=0, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (and squeezed_down_out on gelatin_box). On the stock hinge (axis 81 mm above the fingertip), the moving fingertip rises as the jaw opens and its face tilts. Measured at the failing openings: 78 mm gives tip +17 mm; 80-86 mm gives tip +18 to +23 mm, face pushing 60-85 deg down. Objects that are 30-45 mm tall have their tops at only +15 to +23 mm, so the moving jaw lands on the top face, or on the top edge pushing 33 deg down. Every failing object is at least 73 mm wide, and every held object at most 75 mm.
proposals.principle: A tilted contact pushes the object down with N sin a, and friction mu N must resist it. A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q). Tilting the moving pad back moves the opening where it is parallel out to a wide opening and pulls the contact point down. The TPU skin raises mu from 0.45 to 0.9, so any remaining tilt below about 40 deg (tan a < mu) holds instead of squeezing the object out.
proposals.hypothesis: Brief numbers for pads at pad_angle_deg=45: at 85 mm the face is +14 deg (stock +53) and the tip is +14 mm (stock +23); at 55 mm the face is -8 deg and the tip -5 mm. For the tuna can (top at +17), a contact at about +14 mm on a 14 deg face with mu 0.9 is a side grip, not a press on the top. For the gelatin box at 73-78 mm, the interpolated values are a face of about +5 deg and a tip of about +8 mm, under its +15 mm top. The pudding box at about 90 mm is marginal: the tip is near +18 mm against a +19 mm top. Params alone cannot do this, because System 1 already searched close/side/depth and the rise is fixed by the hinge geometry. The other jaw options are worse. Parallelogram link 90 keeps the face vertical, but its tip rises +33 mm at 85 mm, which is worse than stock. Long_slide at sector 50 is flat, but the brief predicts the rack lifts 2.2 mm off the gear at 85 mm (teeth skip past 0.5) and the bushings carry 138 N against a 52.9 N rating, so it would fail exactly at the openings that matter. Pads cost $0, 0 days and 18 machine minutes. The 1.5 mm groove is there so the round held objects stay centred on the new pad faces.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube, flat_screwdriver: at 17-35 mm openings the 45 deg pad gives a face of about -21 to -27 deg (bottom swung in) and puts the moving tip 10-12 mm below the fixed one. They should survive for two reasons. First, tan 27 deg = 0.51 is below the TPU mu of 0.9, so the upward push is held by friction. Second, System 1 can raise grasp.depth so the lower moving tip clears the table, and these are flat-sided prisms, so a contact above the middle is fine. This is still the main risk.

apple, tomato_soup_can, banana (70-75 mm): the face moves from about +44 deg to about +5 deg and the tip drops, which should only help. The heavy cans (349-370 g) gain from mu 0.9 against the metal's 0.35 (contact friction is set by the softer pad).

round objects (golf_ball, plum, lemon, racquetball, strawberry, tennis_ball): their contacts move to the TPU pads. The groove centres them, and the face is nearer vertical at 42-66 mm (about -10 to +3 deg), so equator contacts should hold.
mustard_bottle (96 mm) is past the 95 mm maximum opening with these pads, so it is not expected to gain; it is not a held group.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing two settings of the stock pads part and no jaw swap. On the stock hinge, the moving fingertip rises and its face tilts as the jaw opens wide. The failing objects are all at least 73 mm wide and only 30-58 mm tall, so the moving jaw lands on their top face. Tilted pads with a TPU skin change the contact angle and how high the contact sits, at no cost ($0, 0 days, 18 machine minutes).

Why not the other jaws:
- Parallelogram (link 90): the moving fingertip rises even more, +33 mm at 85 mm.
- Prismatic / long_slide: at wide openings the brief predicts the gear teeth skip and the bushings are overloaded (138-260 N against a 52.9 N rating).
- 12 V servos ($68 to buy against $40 left): refused, and not needed. The 514 g sugar box needs about 1.18 N*m at the shoulder against a 1.62 N*m stall.

Purchases: none. If wide objects are still blocked after this, the next step would be a slide with stiffer guides, which would be an idea rather than a catalogue part, because the bench has no linear rail (mgn7_rail).

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (and squeezed_down_out on gelatin_box). The stock jaw's fingertip rises as the jaw swings open: +17 to +23 mm above the fixed tip at the 78-86 mm closures logged. That is above the tops of the tuna can (+17), pudding box (+19) and sugar box (+23) and level with the gelatin box top (+15). So the moving jaw presses down at 73-85 deg, and on the gelatin box at 33 deg.
proposals.principle: A face that turns with its joint is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only, and a fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q). Tilting the moving pad back 45 deg moves the parallel opening out to the wide objects and pulls the tip down. The brief for pad_angle_deg=45 gives 85 mm: face +14 deg, tip +14 mm (stock +53 deg, +23 mm), and 55 mm: face -8 deg, tip -5 mm. A contact below the top with a 14 deg tilt is a side grip: tan 14 = 0.25, well under the 0.9 friction of a TPU skin.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the same 45 deg pad as iteration 1's first proposal, with the refusal causes removed. That pad was refused only on mechanism law: two pads overlapped by about 0.1 mm when the jaw was nearly closed (-0.16..-0.07 rad), and the fixed pad's screw did not reach the jaw. Both point to pad thickness. With a 2 mm TPU skin on each face plus a 1.5 mm groove, the faces are 4+ mm thicker in total, which closes a gap of tenths of a mm and puts the screw out of reach of the jaw. Halving the skin to 1 mm removes 2 mm from the closing direction, about 20x the 0.1 mm overlap. Dropping the groove removes the extra thickness it needs. Friction stays at 0.9, which the round held objects need because the tilted pad meets them at -15 to -24 deg near 42-47 mm. Wide objects interpolated: pudding (90 mm) tip about +18 vs top +19 (marginal); sugar (92) about +19 vs top +23; mustard (96) about +23, below its +29 widest point, so the push is up, which friction 0.9 resists; tuna (85) +14 vs top +17; gelatin (73) about +6 vs top +15 with the face near parallel. No catalogue jaw does this: the parallelogram's tip rises more (+33 mm at 85), the prismatic slide tops out at 68 mm, and the long slide's rack skips its teeth at 85 mm with overloaded bushings. Bill of materials: m2_screw x4 on hand, 2 g PLA, 1 g TPU; $0, 0 days, about 18 min.
risks: golf_ball, strawberry, plum: at 42-53 mm the 45 deg pad meets a sphere at about -10 to -24 deg, below its equator, pushing it up by N sin(a). tan 24 = 0.45 is under the 0.9 TPU friction, and System 1 can re-tune depth, so they should survive.

dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube, flat_screwdriver: the moving tip sits about 10 mm below the fixed tip at 17-35 mm and could reach the table. On box-shaped objects the tilted pad's edge pushes on a vertical side, so the contact force is horizontal. System 1 can raise the grasp depth. The loop's parameter refits can lower pad_angle if needed.
apple, banana, tomato_soup_can: maximum opening drops from 99 to about 95 mm, still clear of 75 mm, and their faces become nearer parallel (about +0 to +10 deg instead of +44).

idea.name: braced long slide
idea.description: The long_slide jaw (sector radius 50 mm: up to 103 mm opening, face parallel, tip +1 mm, 32 N at every width), changed to remove its two failure modes. idea.name: rocker pad (convex-crowned jaw pad)
idea.description: A printed pad whose face, seen from the side, is a circular arc of about 40 mm radius spanning normals from about -25 deg to +65 deg on the moving jaw, with a TPU skin. A flat wedge is parallel to the fixed face at only one opening. On a convex face, the point whose normal is horizontal always exists, so the contact on a vertical box side is antipodal (no N sin a squeeze-out) at every opening from 17 to 95 mm. The arc runs down to the pad's lowest point, so at wide openings (where the jaw has turned 45-60 deg) the horizontal-normal point sits near the bottom of the pad. That puts the contact below the tops of low wide objects (pudding +19, tuna +17, sugar +23), while at narrow openings the contact moves up the pad and the heel stays out of the way (fixes the banana conflict). A lower arc, kept within the jaw's footprint, gives mustard the fingertip drop it needs at 96 mm, provided the opening stays at or above the stock 95 mm.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing three changes, all to the pad's tilt angle; nothing needs to be bought. The current pads are tilted 30°, and every body tilted 39.6° or more has lost the banana, so these three test steps in between: 33°, 36° and 38°.

**Why the four objects fail.** On a hinged jaw the moving face is parallel to the fixed one at only one opening, roughly where the jaw has turned by the pad's tilt angle. The four failing objects need openings of 85–96 mm. There the moving face is 29–35° off parallel, so its upper edge presses down on the box's top corner instead of squeezing its side.

**The trade-off.** Tilting the pad further makes the face more parallel at wide openings. It also drops the moving fingertip by about 0.6 mm per degree. The record shows the cost: from 39.6° up, that lower fingertip hits the banana on the way down at its 70 mm opening. The one tested body at 39.6° gained pudding and tuna, and bodies at 42.8° and above also gained sugar.

**What each step should gain.** All three keep the current 1.5 mm rubber (TPU) skin, which has twice the grip of bare plastic. The 39.6° body had no skin, so it should tolerate more tilt than that body did:
- **33°:** tuna only, and only just.
- **36°:** tuna and pudding.
- **38°:** sugar as well, but it is the most likely to lose the banana.

All three change the same part, so each is tried on its own. Together they also show at what angle the banana starts to fail.

**What none of them can do.**
- **Mustard bottle:** it is 96 mm wide, beyond the jaw's 94–95 mm maximum opening with any pad tilt. The only catalogue part that opens wide enough lifts its fingertip 47 mm at an 85 mm opening.
- **Slide jaws:** both are overloaded at wide openings. The gear teeth skip by up to 3.0 mm against a 0.5 mm limit, and the bearings carry 138 N against a 52.9 N rating.
- **Stronger arm servos:** these cost $68 against the $40 left, and the arm has torque to spare: about 1.18 of 1.62 N·m at the heaviest object, 514 g.

If no flat tilt holds both the banana and the wide boxes, the fix is the curved (rocker) pad already recorded as an idea. It costs nothing from the manifest but can't be built in the simulator yet.

At the wide openings these objects need (85–92 mm), the hinged moving face is 20–29°+ off parallel with the bottom swung out (75 mm: 20°, 85 mm: 29°) and its fingertip is 14–23 mm higher than the fixed one. proposals.principle: Two contacts hold only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at one opening only. No single flat pad angle satisfies both the banana (it needs ≤30°: every angle from 33° to 45° lost it, across 8 trials) and the wide boxes (they need about 40–45°: b020 and b011 gained pudding, sugar and tuna). A face that turns to match the object, rather than one fixed to the jaw, removes this trade-off.
proposals.hypothesis:
Self-aligning moving pad. The moving pad carries its TPU face on a pivot pin whose axis runs horizontally along the pad width and lies in the contact surface, about 5 mm above the toe. A TPU flexure centres the face at the current 30° wedge pose, and hard stops allow ±35°. When a box side meets the tilted face, its edge contact sits off the pivot and makes a large moment, so the face rotates flat against the wall: the normal becomes horizontal and antipodal to the fixed face. Squeeze stays 20 N, and with TPU friction against cardboard or metal the hold is 2·0.35–0.5·20 = 14–20 N against 1.7–5 N of weight. On round objects, and on the banana, the contact falls at or near the pivot, so the moment is small, the flexure keeps the 30° pose, and the behaviour stays that of the held body.

The catalogue cannot do this, and the brief's numbers show why:
- pads params: 5 parameter trials gained 0. Angles 33–45° lose the banana. Reach 8 or 16 mm lost potted_meat_can and gained nothing, because added length also adds to the R(1−cos q) rise.
- parallelogram: the fingertip rises +47 mm at 85 mm (link 90). Link 50 reaches only 57 mm.
- prismatic: opens at most 60 mm.
- long_slide (sector 50): opens 95 mm with the tip at +3 mm, but each bushing carries 138 N against a 52.9 N rating, and the rack lifts 3.0 mm off the gear at 85 mm (teeth skip past 0.5 mm). It would fail exactly at the boxes' widths. The braced version is already recorded as an idea.
- servos_12v: refused at $68 against $40 left, and torque is not the mechanism.

It also differs from the recorded rocker pad. A crown sets the contact angle by geometry, but a pivoting face takes the angle from the object's own wall and gives an area contact on flat sides.

Mustard_bottle is 96 mm across, beyond the revolute jaw's 94 mm maximum (95 mm at a 45° pad), so this pad cannot gain it. That needs a jaw that opens wider.

round objects held now (golf_ball, plum, lemon, strawberry, tennis_ball, apple, racquetball, tomato_soup_can): a free pad on a sphere could tilt its normal off the equator. Putting the pivot axis in the contact surface means a centred contact makes no moment, so the face holds its current 30° behaviour.

dice, wood_block_cube, large_marker (17–26 mm): the face is 16–22° off with the bottom swung in. A box side will rotate it flat, which is closer to antipodal than now, but the 5 mm pivot height above the toe must stay below the 17 mm dice top. It does.

idea.name: self-aligning pivot pad (moving jaw)
idea.description: A replacement for the moving-jaw pad. A printed PLA shoe bolts to the moving jaw with the existing 4 m2 screws at the current 30° wedge. A separate printed face plate with a 1.5 mm TPU skin pivots on an m3 screw used as a pin, running through a printed bushing. The pivot axis is horizontal along the 12 mm pad width and lies in the contact plane about 5 mm above the toe. A printed TPU flexure, two 1 mm webs between shoe and plate, centres the plate at the 30° pose, with hard stops at ±35°. The fixed pad stays as it is, since its face is already vertical. When a flat side presses an edge of the tilted plate, the off-pivot load rotates the plate flat against the wall, so the contact normal is horizontal at any opening. A contact at the pivot, as on spheres, makes no moment and keeps the 30° behaviour that holds the current 17 groups. Added wrist mass is about 4 g.
idea.test: In the gripper model, split the moving pad into two bodies. The shoe stays fixed to the moving jaw at pad_angle_deg=30. The face plate (TPU friction 0.9, 1.5 mm skin) is joined to it by a hinge whose axis runs along the pad width and lies on the face surface 5 mm above the toe. Give the hinge a torsional spring of about 0.05 N·m/rad centred at 0, joint limits ±35°, and light damping. Run all 21 groups, re-tuning with System 1, and check the no-interference law for the plate against the fixed pad over the -0.17..1.20 rad range of the jaw.

iterations.notes:
The four failing objects share one cause: the revolute jaw's fingertip rises as it opens, and at their widths it ends up level with or above their tops. They need a jaw that slides straight, so I'm proposing two versions of the catalogue long_slide in place of the revolute jaw.

**Diagnosis.** The traces show the moving fingertip 15–22 mm above the fixed one at 76–84 mm openings. The box tops sit at +17 to +23 mm, so the moving pad lands on the top face and pushes 80–86° down, and the fixed jaw never loads the side. The mustard bottle (96 mm) is also wider than the current 94 mm maximum opening.

**Why a swap, and why this part.**
- The five pad-parameter trials gained nothing. Pad angles of 33–45° fix the wide boxes but always lose the banana, and reach 8–16 mm loses the potted meat can.
- The parallelogram jaw makes the rise worse (+47 mm at 85 mm), and the prismatic jaw only opens to 60 mm.
- Only long_slide keeps the fingertip level (+3 mm at every opening) and opens to 95 mm. I set it to the 50 mm sector radius, the widest it goes. With the pad angle at 0° the faces should be parallel.

**The slide's weak point.** The brief says the steel rods bend under load. At the full 32 N squeeze, the rack lifts 0.8 mm off the gear at 55 mm and 3.0 mm at 85 mm, and teeth skip past 0.5 mm. The bushings also take 138 N against a 52.9 N rating. This only works if System 1's close target keeps the squeeze below the skip point. By my estimate that limit is about 5 N at 85–90 mm, and the bushing load then drops below its rating too:
- **Pudding box** (about 1.8 N needed) and **tuna can** (about 2.4 N) fit comfortably.
- **Sugar box** (2.8–5 N) is marginal.
- **Tomato soup can** is the tightest of the held objects (about 7 N needed against a roughly 10 N limit at 68 mm).

**The two proposals.**
1. Long slide with the current 1.5 mm TPU skin. I expect it to gain the pudding box, the tuna can and probably the sugar box.
2. Same slide with a 0.5 mm skin, which should open about 2 mm wider (to about 97 mm) so the mustard bottle fits, with the same 0.9 friction. The bottle may still slip, because it needs about 3–5 N and only about 4 N is available before teeth skip at that width.

**Cost.** Either version buys two 3 x 150 mm steel rods and two linear bushings: $6.40, 3 days lead, about 225 machine minutes. That fits in the $40, 7 days and 591 minutes left. Holding the sugar box loads the shoulder to about 1.3 N·m, under the 1.62 N·m stall.

**If the trial shows teeth skipping on the wide held objects,** a stiffer slide is needed. That is the "braced long slide" idea already recorded, so it's the next step and I haven't proposed it again here.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on pudding_box, sugar_box and tuna_fish_can (and mustard_bottle, which also needs more than 94 mm of opening). At the openings these objects need (85 to 92 mm, servo 1.04 to 1.12 rad), the moving face is 20 to 29 deg off parallel with its bottom swung out, and the moving fingertip sits +15 to +23 mm above the fixed one. Because the bottom is swung out, the upper part of the face lies further inward than the toe. The box's top corner meets that face (or the toe) first, and the contact pushes 80 to 86 deg down: 23 N at +17 to +20 mm with the top at +19 to +23. The fixed jaw gets no contact, so the hand stalls or trips the force limit (tuna 13 to 17 N down on its top).
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only. Any single pad wedge angle therefore trades the narrow and mid openings against the wide ones. The record shows this: 30 deg holds the banana but leaves the wide boxes at +20 to +29 deg, and 33 to 45 deg fixes the boxes but loses the banana. A pad whose orientation is held vertical by a linkage, instead of being set by the jaw angle, is parallel at every opening.
proposals.hypothesis:
Levelled moving pad. Keep the stock revolute jaw: same hinge, R = 81 mm, 1.37 rad span, 94 mm max opening, about 20 N squeeze. Replace the fixed-wedge moving pad with a pad carrier that turns on a pin (MR63 bearing) at the moving fingertip. A printed levelling link runs from the top of the carrier to a second pin (MR63) on the gripper body, offset from the servo hinge by the same vector as pivot to carrier-top. Together they form a parallelogram on the stock jaw, so the TPU face stays vertical at every jaw angle.

Why the catalogue cannot do this. pads/pad_angle: five trials and the b011/b020 family, a single angle cannot meet both the banana and the boxes. parallelogram: its links pivot at the servo axis, so the tip rises +47 mm at 85 mm (link 90), twice the stock +23, which would lose gelatin, banana and apple. prismatic and long_slide: the brief computes rack lift of 0.8 to 3.0 mm past the 0.5 mm skip limit and bushing loads of 138 to 260 N against a 52.9 N rating at 55 to 85 mm, and sector radius 50 was refused for hitting the wrist. servos_12v: refused at $68 against $40 left. It also fixes torque, not geometry: sugar at 514 g needs 0.41 + 0.77 = 1.18 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall.

Why this differs from the recorded ideas. The self-aligning pivot pad is passive: it turns to whatever it touches first, which here is the box's top corner, so it would align to the corner. The rocker pad only reshapes the face. The levelled pad is driven vertical before contact. With the face vertical, the top corner can only meet the face if the toe is above the top. At the System 1 depths already found (15 to 26 mm below the top), the stock toe rise of +17 to +22 mm puts the toe at or a few mm below the top: tuna about 3 mm below, pudding about 8 mm, sugar about 4 mm. That makes the contact a horizontal one on the wall. Even a 3 mm band of TPU contact holds tuna: 171 g needs about 1.7 N, and 2 x 0.35 x 20 N = 14 N. Sugar (514 g) needs about 5 N with lift margin, against 2 x 0.5 x 20 = 20 N. Narrow objects go from -22 deg (bottom in) to exactly antipodal. The toe height is unchanged from stock at narrow openings (-3 mm). Mustard at 96 mm stays beyond the 94 mm opening, so I do not claim it.
risks: banana: it is held now with the 30 deg wedge at about 70 mm, where the face is about +17 deg. With the face vertical the contact becomes antipodal on its 38 mm-tall side, and the toe is +14 to +17 mm above the fixed one, below the 38 mm top. It should survive, but the banana has been lost by every change to the moving face so far, and some of those losses happened at t=0.02 s. The link must clear the banana at the start pose.

dice and large_marker: these are now held with the face 22 deg bottom-in, which lifts them slightly. A vertical face is the ideal antipodal contact and the toe stays at -3 mm. The carrier pivot must not foul the fixed pad shoe at the closed pose (-0.17 rad), the interference that refused the lip and reach-8 trials.
potted_meat_can (370 g, metal 0.35): at 57 mm the face goes from about +6 deg to 0 deg, a small change and a safe one.

the round objects (apple, golf_ball, lemon, plum, racquetball, strawberry, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can): they are held at the equator. A vertical face with the toe below the equator gives a horizontal contact at the equator. Apple at 75 mm has its toe at +14 mm, and its equator at +36 mm above the table is above the toe.

idea.name: levelled moving pad (pad-levelling link on the stock revolute jaw)
idea.description: A printed pad carrier carries the TPU-faced moving pad and turns on a 3 mm pin with an MR63 bearing at the stock moving fingertip. The jaw, the link, the carrier and the body form a parallelogram, so the pad face keeps a vertical orientation at every servo angle from -0.17 to 1.20 rad. idea.name: mid-arc parallelogram jaw (offset-hung finger, sag-balanced)
idea.description: Two printed 100 mm links run from the gripper servo horn and from a second frame pivot, offset parallel to it, to a coupler. This is a four-bar parallelogram, so the moving finger never rotates and its face stays parallel to the fixed jaw at every opening. The difference from the catalogue parallelogram: the finger is an L-bracket hung from the coupler about 28 mm toward the open side, and the horn is indexed so the links are vertical when the jaws are 58.5 mm apart. The fingertip then runs along the lowest part of its 100 mm circle across the whole 17–100 mm working range, rising at most 9 mm between the middle and either end. The finger's toe is extended 4.5 mm below that lowest point, which splits the remaining error into ±4.5 mm against the fixed fingertip. The face is a flat vertical TPU-skinned pad (the existing pads at pad_angle 0, groove 0, 12 mm wide). Maximum opening is 100 mm (mustard is 96 mm). Squeeze is servo torque over L cos θ, about 16–18 N. Each pivot runs on an MR63 bearing pair on an M3 screw.
idea.test: A parallelogram jaw variant in the simulator with two extra geometry parameters. The first is the finger's horizontal offset from the coupler (or, equivalently, the opening at which the links are vertical), range 30–70 mm. Mechanism-law checks are needed for link sweep against the wrist at every wrist roll (the long_slide sector failed this) and for the finger against the fixed jaw at the closed end. No revolute setting fixes this: the brief gives tip +14 mm at 75 mm and +23 mm at 85 mm with the face 29 deg off, and tuna's top is at +17 mm. Pad angles of 33-45 deg lost the banana, and reach 8-16 mm lost potted_meat_can. The parallelogram is worse (+47 mm tip at 85 mm with link 90), and 12 V does not address the mechanism and is unaffordable ($68 vs $40). long_slide holds tip +3 mm at every opening; with pad angle 0 the face should be parallel. Both earlier slide trials were refused at sector 50, with the same wrist-pinion overlap (1.6 x 0.2 x 0.5 mm at -0.17 rad) at TPU 1.5 and 0.5. So TPU did not cause it, and this changes the radius instead: 49.7 mm should pull the sector in about 0.3 mm against the 0.2 mm overlap. That margin is thin. Opening, fitted linearly from the brief's 60 mm at r=30 and 95 mm at r=50, is about 1.75r + 7.5 = 94.5 mm. TPU 0.4 adds about 2.2 mm (1.1 mm per face), giving about 96.7 mm against the mustard's 96 mm. Squeeze is about 33 N at stall. Sugar needs about 5 N of weight support plus margin, so System 1 can close gently, well under stall. Cost $6.40, 3 days, about 216 machine min for the slide, plus a few minutes to reprint the pads; all within budget.
risks: All held groups: the 0.3 mm interference margin may not clear, or TPU 0.4 may be too thin for the part's rules. Either would be refused before trial at no build cost.

potted_meat_can and tomato_soup_can (370 g and 349 g, friction 0.35): at stall the brief shows rack lift of about 0.8 mm at 55 mm opening (skip limit 0.5) and 138 N per bushing (rated 52.9). They survive only if System 1 finds a close target near 10 N, about 40% of the stall load scale.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding, sugar, mustard) and force_limit with the pad pressing on the top (tuna): at these openings the moving toe has risen to or above the object's top.
proposals.principle: A finger can only hold an object's side if its fingertip reaches below the object's top at that object's opening. proposals.hypothesis: The brief gives +23 mm tip rise and a 29 deg face at 85 mm on the 30 deg wedge, against tops at +17 (tuna), +19 (pudding) and +23 (sugar). At 45 deg the same opening gives +14 mm and 14 deg, and the b011 family gained all these wide boxes except mustard. The cost there was banana. Banana's only non-30-degree-like survivor in the record is reach 16 (it held at 30 deg), so this pairs reach 16 with 45 deg, a combination not yet tried. Reach 16 at 30 deg lost potted_meat_can with a pad pressing on its top at +42 mm. My reading is that at 57 mm the 30 deg face leans about 6 deg with its bottom out, so its upper part overhangs the can, and a longer pad makes that worse. At 45 deg the face at 57 mm is bottom-in by about 7 deg, so it should not overhang. The earlier r6 potted failure (squeezed_down_out, tip -7 mm) was on bare PLA, which I believe is the b01t10 base. Keeping TPU 1.5 (friction 0.9) gives margin against that tilt. Reach also adds about 16 sin(face) mm of opening at the same servo angle, so maximum opening should go from 95 to about 100 mm and the 96 mm mustard would at least fit, though its roughly 24 deg face probably will not hold it. Cheaper moves are used up: angle alone and reach alone have failed. Catalogue swaps do not help either. Parallelogram rises +47 mm at 85 mm. long_slide lost 17 groups to rack lift of 1.2-1.4 mm and bushing overload (138 N against 52.9 N rated at r=50). prismatic reaches only 60 mm. servos_12v costs $68 against $40 left and does not address tip rise.

flat_screwdriver, wood_block_cube: narrow objects grip with the steepest bottom-in face (about 21 deg at 35 mm), and the longer toe drops further below the fixed one, so the object may be squeezed up.

proposals.edit: pads (width_mm=8)
proposals.mechanism: force_limit and fixed_jaw_missed on banana, the single held group that blocks the 45 deg wedge from fixing moving_jaw_on_top_face on the wide boxes.
proposals.principle: Every change to a part can alter what the hand already does well. A pad is a contact patch: on a curved 198 mm object, a wide pad meets the bow off-centre and can turn or jam the object instead of closing on it.
proposals.hypothesis: b020 (45 deg, bare PLA, width 10) would gain gelatin, pudding, sugar and tuna and lost only banana, so its other held groups are the best evidence in the record. Width affects banana's failure mode. At widths 14.3, 16 and 24 one placement reads fixed_jaw_missed, with the moving jaw stopped at 86 mm and the fixed jaw not touching. At width 10 that reading disappears, replaced by a 10 N side contact at -4 mm and force_limit. The trend suggests a narrower pad catches less of the banana's curve, so width 8, the bottom of the range, is the untested end of that trend. Bare PLA stays because b020 held the rest on it, and because lower friction lets the banana slip into place rather than jam. The t=0.02 s force_limit reading on the other placement may not respond to width, and it is the most likely reason this fails. Everything else in pads has been tried on this base: width 24, reach 3.2 and 6, while groove 3 was refused.
risks: banana: this is the group the proposal exists to save, and it remains the most likely loss. The t=0.02 s force_limit placement has no clear link to pad width.

potted_meat_can, tomato_soup_can: these are heavy, low-friction metal objects (370 g and 349 g at friction 0.35) on bare PLA. A narrower pad gives less contact and less margin, and tilt is less tolerated without TPU.
flat_screwdriver, large_marker: long objects have less resistance to turning about the grip axis on an 8 mm pad, though they are light (70 g and 16 g).

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=1.5)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on tuna, pudding and sugar, which b020 fixes; the remaining blocker is banana's force_limit (10 N on its side at t=2.37 s, plus the contact at t=0.02 s).
proposals.principle: A concave or grooved contact locates a rounded flank across the pad. A face parallel to the fixed one at a wider opening keeps the moving fingertip below the top of a wide box.
proposals.hypothesis: b020 (45 deg wedge, bare PLA, width 10) gains gelatin, pudding, sugar and tuna in the record, and loses only banana. Gelatin is already held, so the net gain would be three groups. The brief puts the 45 deg wedge at +14 mm and 14 deg at 85 mm, against +23 mm and 29 deg now, and tops at +17 (tuna), +19 (pudding) and +23 (sugar). The other pad levers on this family are spent: widths 8 to 24 and reach 3.2, 6 and 16 mm all still lost banana. Groove is the one lever never trialled on it, because groove 3 was refused. That refusal showed a 2.8 mm frame overlap against the 2 mm allowed and a 0.1 mm shoe overlap. If overlap scales with depth, 1.5 mm gives about 1.3 mm of frame overlap and should clear the frame and shoe limits; the mount refusal may or may not clear with it. A shallow V may stop the banana flank sliding along the face. It does not obviously explain the t=0.02 s contact, so this is a test and not a confident fix. No jaw swap can do this job: the parallelogram tip is +47 mm at 85 mm, prismatic stops at 60 mm, and long_slide lost all 17 groups to rack lift. It costs no purchases, about 18 machine minutes (2 g PLA, 1 g TPU only if a skin is used; less here), and reuses the m2 screws.
risks: banana: it has failed on every wedge of 33 deg or more, and this is the most likely loss.
dice, large_marker and flat_screwdriver: a groove on a 10 mm pad narrows the flat contact. b020 held them, and width 8 lost flat_screwdriver, so the margin is not large.
potted_meat_can: it is bare PLA on metal at 370 g. b020 held it, and a shallow groove should change little, but it lost it at width 8.

proposals.edit: pads (pad_tpu_mm=0.4)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on the wide boxes through the 45 deg wedge, while addressing banana's sliding contact at force_limit (10 N on its side at t=2.37 s).
proposals.principle: Friction resists the push of a tilted contact: a contact tilted by a holds only while mu N exceeds N sin(a). A TPU skin raises friction to 0.9 from bare PLA's 0.45.
proposals.hypothesis: The record has tried 45 deg with TPU 0 at several widths, and 45 deg with TPU 1.5 only at reach 16, which lost potted_meat_can to the reach. It has not visibly tried a thin skin at width 10 and reach 0. A 0.4 mm skin adds only 0.8 mm across the two faces, so b020's wide-box geometry barely moves, while friction doubles if the 0.9 figure holds at this thickness. The brief does not tie friction to thickness, so that is an assumption. Higher pad friction may keep the banana from sliding and turning along the face during the close. It may also widen the margin on the tilted contacts. 0.4 mm is one nozzle width, so it is printable as a skin. It needs no purchases and about 18 machine minutes (2 g PLA, 1 g TPU).
risks: banana: the t=0.02 s contact is unexplained and friction may not touch it, so this remains the most likely loss.
potted_meat_can and flat_screwdriver: width 8 lost both to squeezed_up_out, and higher friction at width 10 could change how they seat, though it should help hold them.
dice and large_marker: 0.8 mm less opening than b020 at a given servo angle is small against their 17 and 19 mm widths, and the record holds them with thicker skin.

proposals.edit: pads (pad_angle_deg=32, pad_tpu_mm=0.4, reach_mm=3.2)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face and force_limit on tuna: the moving fingertip rises to +23 mm at 85 mm with the face 29 deg off parallel, pressing on the top at +17.
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises as the jaw opens, so anything that reaches the same opening at a smaller servo angle lowers the fingertip and reduces the tilt.
proposals.hypothesis: This stacks three small levers, each kept below the value where the record shows a loss: wedge under the 33 deg where banana starts failing, and reach at the 3.2 mm that b01t10 showed keeps potted_meat_can. Thinning TPU from 1.5 to 0.4 mm adds 2.2 mm of opening. At the brief's 0.9 mm of rise and 0.9 deg per mm of opening, that is about -2 mm and -2 deg. Two more degrees of wedge at 0.6 mm and 1 deg per degree gives -1.2 mm and -2 deg. Reach 3.2 at about 25 deg adds 1.35 mm of opening, for about -0.9 mm net. Estimated result at 85 mm is tip about +18.9 mm and face about 24 deg. With depth 26 mm the fixed toe sits about 9 mm below tuna's centre, so the moving toe lands near +10, about 7 mm under the +17 top, against about 3 mm today. This is a marginal gain: wedges of 33 to 38 deg reportedly gained nothing, and they reach similar tip heights, so only tuna is predicted. It is still the one visible region below 33 deg that has not been tried. It needs no purchases and about 18 machine minutes (2 g PLA, 1 g TPU).
risks: banana: thin TPU and reach shift its opening the same way a larger wedge does, so the effective wedge may pass the 33 deg limit.
potted_meat_can: it lost at reach 6 and 8 mm in other wedges. 3.2 mm held only at 45 deg, so holding at 32 deg is not proven.
gelatin_box, apple and tomato_soup_can: they rely on the current friction and geometry at 68 to 75 mm, and should improve with a lower tip if friction holds at 0.4 mm.

iterations.notes:
Odds are low for all three, and I would treat a kept result as a surprise. No visible trial has both held banana and gained a wide box. Wedges at or above 33 deg lose banana, and the record suggests wide boxes need a tip about as low as a 40 deg wedge gives. Proposals 1 and 2 test the two levers not yet tried on b020. Proposal 3 tests the untried region just under the banana limit, and it predicts tuna only.

Mustard is not predicted by any proposal. At 96 mm it exceeds the stock 94 mm opening, and thin TPU only brings that to about 96 mm, with no clearance and a large tip rise.

The t=0.02 s banana contact is unexplained, and none of these changes clearly addresses it. All numbers marked estimated are my interpolations from the brief's slopes, not simulator output.

Nothing here needs buying. If none is kept, the honest end state is 17/21, and the next step is a simulator builder for the levelled moving pad, recorded at $1.80, which targets the root conflict by holding the face angle independently of the opening. It remains untested.
